summary: Give the Water potential calculator the osmotic potential, the gravitational potential, the hydrostatic potential and the overburden potential and it returns pressure potential (Ψp). Think of it as a shortcut for an animal, a plant or a biological process whose scale you want to put into perspective. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Water potential calculator work?
sections.html:
The Water potential calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports pressure potential (Ψp) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the osmotic potential (Ψo), the gravitational potential (Ψg), the hydrostatic potential (Ψh) and the overburden potential (Ψa).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Water potential calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Pressure potential (Ψp)=Ψ − overburden potential (Ψa) − gravitational potential (Ψg) − hydrostatic potential (Ψh) − matric potential (Ψm) − osmotic potential (Ψo)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in bars, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Water potential calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Supporting a lesson, a lecture or a field note
  • Putting a biological quantity into a scale you can picture
  • Comparing two organisms, populations or processes
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the osmotic potential, the gravitational potential and the hydrostatic potential — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Water potential calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Water potential calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns pressure potential (Ψp), derived from the osmotic potential, the gravitational potential and the hydrostatic potential. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Water potential calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the osmotic potential, the gravitational potential, the hydrostatic potential and the overburden potential, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter osmotic potential (Ψo) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Osmotic potential (Ψo) opens in bars and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Ψ = 0 bar. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Water potential calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
